quote: I'm not selling anything. I'm appointment setting.
stewart_read: The rep never framed the purpose of the call in the opening (no reference to the form, no legitimacy anchor) — so the customer's very next question is 'what are you selling', a sign the intro didn't do its job. The rep's clarification here is defensive, coming after the customer already sensed a pitch rather than being told upfront.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to open with the standard legitimacy frame — reference the form, state the purpose plainly — so the customer isn't left guessing and firing 'what are you selling' 40 seconds in.

quote: And if we can't save you money in the first year and remove that bill, we're not gonna offer anything at all.
stewart_read: This is a blanket guarantee delivered before any bill amount, usage figure, or utility company was captured. It reads as an unconditional promise the rep has no data to back, and it directly sets up the customer's three-part demand for actual rates later in the call.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may be reciting an approved script line ('bill swap program') verbatim rather than improvising a guarantee — the issue is sequencing (said before qualification) not fabrication.
coaching_implication: Sequence matters: capture the bill/utility first, THEN use the guarantee language once there's a real number to anchor it to. Delivering the promise blind invites exactly the skepticism that followed.

quote: I'm I'm asking what those rates are that you would be paying. It'll always be cheaper than what you're paying now. It can never be higher. But you don't know what I'm paying now.
stewart_read: The customer essentially hands the rep the exact gap he needs to close — 'you don't know what I'm paying now' — which is a direct invitation to ask for the bill amount. The rep does not pick this up; the transcript shows no subsequent question about the customer's actual bill.
coaching_implication: This is the single clearest missed pivot in the call. The rep should have said something like 'you're right, let's fix that — what's your average monthly bill?' instead of repeating the guarantee a second time.

quote: Yeah. But that's why the that's why the bill swap program is so cool because we're gonna keep it under because your power bill is gonna rise no matter what. Our bill will always stay under that no matter what.
stewart_read: The customer raised a real inversion opportunity — rising utility costs from data centers — and the rep gestures at it ('your power bill is gonna rise no matter what') but never turns it into the customer's own reason to act; he stays on the generic 'we'll always be under' claim instead of anchoring to the customer's specific complaint about rate hikes.
coaching_implication: When a customer volunteers the villain (rising rates from data centers) themselves, that's a gift — reflect it back explicitly: 'Exactly — that's the trend working against you, and it's exactly why locking in now protects you from it,' rather than a generic restatement of the program.

quote: So can you send me a link to my email so I can do some reading on your company?
stewart_read: The customer's request to self-research by email, after three unanswered asks for real numbers, is a polite way of ending the live conversation. There is no protocol in the schema that maps cleanly to this specific request; it functions as a soft exit the rep should have countered with a next step, not a procedural objection to overcome.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be read as a genuine research request rather than a brush-off, but the immediate 'Okay. I'll call you back' with no time attached, right after, supports the soft-exit read.
coaching_implication: Don't take the website request as an on-ramp to disengagement. Offer to set a specific callback time or short appointment right there — 'I can send that, and let's grab 15 minutes Thursday so I can also get you real numbers off your bill' — rather than closing with 'thank you, have a great day.'

quote: Okay. I'll call you back. Bye.
stewart_read: The call ends with the customer setting the terms of the next contact and no day/time, hour-block, or handshake language from the rep at all — the button-up section never happens.
coaching_implication: This is the clearest procedural gap on the call: no appointment was attempted or locked. Coach the rep to always attempt a specific day/time before letting the customer close the call, even on a call that started this loosely.

quote: Right. I understand the whole concept, but money still has to be pulled out of the wallet. So that's what we're talking about.
stewart_read: This is a direct cost objection the script has a canonical redirect for (grab qualifying info, promise a real design instead of a ballpark), but the rep never uses that redirect — he just restates that a bill will exist, which doesn't answer the customer's actual question.
coaching_implication: Deploy the scripted redirect here: acknowledge the question is fair, then pivot to 'let me grab a few details so I can get you real numbers instead of a guess' — which also would have opened the door to capturing the bill.
